The popular initiative would have the following different effects on the mentioned groups:

*   **Pensioners:** This group would receive an annual supplement in the amount of one-twelfth of their annual pension (p. 2, p. 3). This would improve their financial situation (p. 2, p. 12).
*   **Recipients of IV pensions or survivors' pensions:** These individuals would not receive a supplement (p. 8, p. 9).

**Consequences of this differentiation:**
*   **Different pension amounts:** Within the 1st pillar, the effectively paid-out pensions (AHV old-age pensions compared to IV and survivors' pensions) would differ (p. 8). The Federal Council evaluates this as a new, objectively unjustified unequal treatment of the insured persons in the 1st pillar (p. 9).
*   **Effects on supplementary benefits:** Persons receiving supplementary benefits for IV or survivors' pensions would be financially worse off than pensioners with supplementary benefits, since only the latter would receive the supplement (p. 8, p. 11).
*   **Failure to achieve the objective:** Since recipients of IV pensions are more often dependent on supplementary benefits than pensioners, the Federal Council is of the opinion that the initiative's goal of improving the situation for the poorest individuals is missed (p. 18).

In the event of the adoption of the initiative, the old-age and survivors' insurance (AHV) finances would be affected as follows in the year 2032:

*   **Expenditure:** The expenditure of the AHV would increase by around 5 billion francs (p. 2, 10, 19).
*   **Revenue:** Since the federal contribution to the AHV is linked to the expenditure, the revenue of the AHV would increase by around 1 billion francs (p. 10).
*   **Accounting result:** As a consequence, the accounting result would deteriorate by almost 4 billion francs (p. 10).
*   **Accounting deficit:** The accounting deficit would amount to around 8.7 billion francs in the year 2032 (p. 10).
*   **Scenario with AHV 21:** If the reform AHV 21 were implemented and the initiative adopted at the same time, the accounting deficit would amount to around 6.6 billion francs in the year 2032 (p. 10).

The initiative committee justifies the necessity of a surcharge on AHV old-age pensions with the following points:

*   **Inadequate financial security:** Current AHV old-age pensions are too small for low to medium income classes to guarantee adequate security when transitioning into retirement (p. 4). As evidence, the committee cites that half of the individuals who retired in 2018 had to make do with less than 1772 francs per month and almost every tenth person required supplementary benefits directly after pensioning (p. 4).
*   **Deficiencies in occupational pension provision (2nd pillar) and 3rd pillar:** Individuals with low incomes, especially women, are more reliant on AHV because they often have poorer security in the 2nd pillar (e.g., through part-time work or lower wages) and were able to save less retirement capital (p. 5). Furthermore, pension fund rents have been declining for around ten years (p. 6). The 3rd pillar is hardly an option for individuals with low and medium incomes (p. 6).
*   **Declining replacement rate:** Due to the mechanism of the pension index, pensions generally grow less strongly than wages, which leads to the AHV's replacement rate sinking over time (p. 4, 5).
*   **Rising costs:** Pensioners need an increasingly large part of their pension for additional health costs as well as rising health insurance premiums (p. 5).

From the Federal Council's point of view, a supplement for AHV old-age pensioners would be problematic from the perspective of generational justice (p. 18). The Federal Council justifies this as follows:

*   Today's and future gainfully employed individuals must bear an increasingly higher burden in order to secure the existing level of benefits (p. 18).
*   These burdens are higher than those that the majority of today's pension recipients had to bear during their gainful employment (p. 18).
*   It is therefore questionable whether today's old-age pensioners should be granted a supplement to their ongoing pensions, which they themselves have not financed or have only financed to a small extent (p. 18).

The Federal Council predicts that the additional expenditures of the AHV in the year 2032 would reach around 5 billion francs (p. 2, 10, 19). According to Annex 3, these additional expenditures amount concretely to 5'011 million francs (p. 26).

The initiative committee proposes to finance the additional expenditure for the surcharge through the following sources:
*   an increase in the wage contributions of employees and employers (p. 8)
*   the use of part of the profits of the National Bank (p. 8, p. 14)
The popular initiative "For a better life in old age (initiative for a 13th AHV pension)" has been launched with 101,793 valid signatures (p. 3).

According to the synthesis survey social security and labour market (SESAM) from the year 2019, 26 percent of the OASI pension recipients (without pension-receiving partners) receive a maximum pension (p. 16).

The Federal Council recommends rejecting the initiative for the following reasons:

*   **Financial risks:** The annual additional expenditures of the old-age and survivors' insurance (AHV) would reach around 5 billion francs by 2032 (p. 2, p. 10). This would exacerbate the existing contribution deficit (due to increasing life expectancy and the "baby boomer" generation); the deficit would increase from an estimated 4.7 billion francs to around 8.7 billion francs by 2032 (p. 2, p. 10).
*   **Social injustice and lack of targeting:** A surcharge would be hardly or not at all justified from a social policy perspective for pensioners from higher income classes (p. 2). Furthermore, the initiative would create a new unequal treatment within the first pillar, as only old-age pensions, but not disability or survivor's pensions, would be increased (p. 2, p. 9, p. 18).
*   **Contradiction to needs-based orientation:** The surcharge would contradict the constitutionally mandated needs-based orientation of supplementary benefits (EL) (p. 10). Recipients of EL old-age pensions would be better off than other EL recipients and would receive more than their calculated needs (p. 10).
*   **Existence secured already:** The Federal Council is of the opinion that the constitutional task of securing existence is already fulfilled today through supplementary benefits (p. 8, p. 9, p. 16, p. 23).
*   **Compensation by the second pillar:** The effect of the declining AHV replacement rate would relativize in the overall view, as the development in occupational pension provision (second pillar) would partially compensate for the declining replacement rate of the first pillar (p. 9, p. 16).
*   **Intergenerational justice:** It is argued that today's and future gainfully employed individuals must bear an increasingly heavy burden. It is questionable whether current pensioners should be granted a surcharge that they themselves have hardly financed (p. 18).
*   **Ongoing reforms:** With the reforms AHV 21 and BVG 21, work is already being done on stabilizing financing and maintaining the level of benefits (p. 23).
*   **Lack of financing:** The initiative does not provide for any financing measures. Financing through contributions would increase labor costs and impair the competitiveness of companies (p. 13, p. 19).

The Federal Council recommends rejecting the initiative, among other things, because it creates unequal treatment within the 1st pillar. Its argumentation is based on the following points:

*   **Unjustified unequal treatment:** Since the Federal Constitution puts old-age, survivors', and disability insurance on an equal footing, an additional payment only for old-age pensions would create a new unequal treatment of the insured under the 1st pillar, for which there is no objective justification (p. 9). It is not comprehensible why different approaches should apply to securing the existence of old-age pensioners than for disability and survivors' pensioners (p. 18).
*   **Disadvantaging other pension recipients:** Recipients of disability, widow's, widower's, and orphan's pensions would be disadvantaged in an unjustified manner (p. 11). Since disability pensioners are more frequently dependent on supplementary benefits (EL), the initiative's goal of helping the poorest people would be missed (p. 18).
*   **Contradiction to needs-based orientation:** The planned treatment of the supplement in the context of supplementary benefits would result in old-age pensioners being better off than other EL recipients, which contradicts the constitutionally stipulated needs-based orientation of supplementary benefits (p. 10).
*   **Financial risks:** The Federal Council states that the additional expenditures would amount to around 5 billion francs by 2032 (p. 2, p. 19). This would exacerbate the financial challenges facing the old-age and survivors' insurance, which already exist due to demographic developments, and pose a risk to financial stability (p. 2, p. 19).
*   **Lack of social policy justification:** Such a supplement would be hardly or not at all socially justified for pensioners from higher income classes (p. 2, p. 23).
*   **Fulfillment of the constitutional mandate:** The Federal Council is of the opinion that the constitutional task of securing existence is already fulfilled today by the system of supplementary benefits and therefore there is no need for an increase in old-age and survivors' insurance benefits (p. 9, p. 23).

In the year 2032, the additional expenditures of the AHV due to the adoption of the initiative would amount to around 5 billion francs (p. 2, 10, 19). The share of the Confederation in these additional expenditures would accordingly amount to around 1 billion francs (p. 10, 14). Overall, the increased burden on the Confederation could be around 3 billion francs if one adds up the increase in the federal contribution and the elimination of the National Bank's distribution (p. 14).

Regarding financing, there are different positions:

*   **The initiative committee** proposes to finance the additional expenditure through an increase in wage contributions from employees, employers, and employees or by using part of the National Bank's profits (p. 8, 14).
*   **The Federal Council** states that if financing is done through today's contributions and the federal share (20.2% of expenditures), the contributions of employers as well as employees and workers would have to be increased by around 0.4 percentage points each in 2032 (p. 12). For the federal share of around 1 billion francs, the Federal Council believes that either additional revenue, savings measures in other areas of responsibility, or an increase in value-added tax of at least 1 percentage point would be necessary (p. 14).

The effects of the 13th AHV pension on pensioners differ according to income class as follows:

*   **Pensioners with low incomes:**
    *   **Objectives and benefits:** The initiative committee is of the opinion that today's AHV pensions are too small for low to medium income classes to guarantee adequate financial security (p. 4). Since these individuals often have poorer coverage in occupational pension provision (2nd pillar), they are more dependent on the AHV (p. 5-6). The goal is for the poorest pensioners to feel an improvement (p. 4, p. 7).
    *   **Concrete effect:** All current and new recipients would be financially better off, which would improve their total income (p. 12). For individuals with low pension fund benefits, the proportion of AHV old-age pension in total income would increase (p. 12).

*   **Pensioners with higher incomes:**
    *   **Effect:** Since the initiative does not differentiate between pension recipients, better-off individuals would also receive a higher pension (p. 12, p. 17).
    *   **Federal Council's assessment:** The Federal Council considers such a supplement for pensioners from higher income classes to be hardly or not at all justified from a social policy perspective (p. 2). It states that due to the lack of differentiation, relatively many resources would be spent on groups that are hardly or not at all dependent on the increase (p. 17).

A cancellation of the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons (AFMP) would, due to the so-called guillotine clause (Art. 25 para. 4 AFMP), lead to the elimination of the Bilateral I agreements (p. 66).

Concretely, this would have the following effects:
* **Automatic elimination:** Six months after notification of the cancellation, all agreements of the Bilateral I affected by this clause would automatically cease to apply (p. 66).
* **Affected agreements:** In addition to the AFMP, the agreements on public procurement, the reduction of technical trade barriers, trade in agricultural products, and land and air transport would also become obsolete (p. 66).
* **Economic consequences:** According to analyses cited by the Federal Council, this elimination would lead to significantly weaker economic growth in Switzerland, as well as losses in terms of legal certainty and a reduction in the attractiveness of the location (p. 66).

The Federal Council assesses the impact of the elimination of the Schengen and Dublin association agreements as very negative, both with regard to general economic development and significant additional financial costs (p. 3, 67).

In detail, the Federal Council mentions the following consequences:

*   **Economic impacts:**
    *   The gross domestic product (GDP) could be 1.6 to 3.7 percent lower by 2030 (p. 67).
    *   Per capita income could decrease by 700 to 1600 francs, depending on the scenario (p. 67).
    *   The tourism sector and border regions would be particularly affected, as systematic border controls would increase and facilitations in travel would cease to apply (p. 67).

*   **Financial impacts:**
    *   **Asylum area:** Annual additional costs of around 220 million francs are expected (p. 67). This is due, among other things, to the fact that no Dublin transfers would be possible anymore and an increase in repeat applications could lead to additional costs between 109 million and 1.1 billion francs per year (p. 67).
    *   **Internal security:** To compensate for the elimination of the agreements, additional annual costs of up to 500 million francs are expected (p. 67). Furthermore, there would be a non-monetary loss of value due to the elimination of automatic data exchange and integration into the European search area (p. 67).

The Federal Council assesses the existing as well as additional strategies and measures as more effective in addressing the challenges of immigration and population growth than the demands of the initiative (p. 64).

In comparison to the initiative, the Federal Council represents the following positions:
* **Inappropriateness of the initiative:** The cancellation of agreements in the area of human rights as well as the waiver of freedom of movement when exceeding the threshold values are not appropriate responses to the challenges (p. 64).
* **Risks:** The initiative would endanger prosperity, impair the functioning of society and put the bilateral path with the EU at risk (p. 2). Furthermore, a rigid population upper limit would restrict the necessary flexibility for mastering future challenges (particularly in the areas of the labour market and demographics) (p. 3, p. 82).
* **Alternative through existing instruments:** Instead of endangering the bilateral path, the Federal Council wants to hold on to proven migration policy and humanitarian principles (p. 4). In particular, it sees in the concretised safeguard clause of the Free Movement of Persons Agreement (FMOPA) a possibility to restrict immigration in justified cases without calling into question the entire agreement and thus the bilateral path (p. 3, p. 81).

The Federal Council rejects the popular initiative for the following reasons:

*   **Economy and prosperity:** The initiative would jeopardize prosperity in Switzerland (p. 2) and have significant financial and economic consequences (p. 4, 82). The Free Movement of Persons Agreement (FZA) is central to the Swiss economy and the securing of jobs (p. 64). Furthermore, due to demographic aging, Switzerland relies on foreign workers (p. 3, 82).
*   **Bilateral relations with the EU:** The bilateral path with the EU would be put at risk (p. 2). A cancellation of the FZA would, due to the guillotine clause, lead to the lapse of further internal market agreements and jeopardize the Schengen and Dublin association agreements (p. 3, 66).
*   **Internal security and asylum law:** An exit from the European security area would significantly complicate the guarantee of internal security (p. 4, 82). Furthermore, the asylum system would have to be expanded and would become more expensive, as Dublin returns would no longer be possible (p. 4).
*   **International credibility:** The renegotiation of international agreements in the field of human rights is considered unrealistic and would jeopardize Switzerland's credibility (p. 3, 72).
*   **Flexibility and society:** The anchoring of a rigid limit in the Federal Constitution would reduce the necessary flexibility to cope with future challenges (p. 3, 72, 82) and impair the functioning of society (p. 2, 82).

The development of immigration to Switzerland is presented in the dispatch as follows:

*   **General trends and drivers:** Immigration is strongly influenced by economic development and the demand of the Swiss economy for labor, as well as demographic aging (p. 26, 29).
*   **Immigration from the EU/EFTA area (FZA):** Since the entry into force of the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons (FZA) in 2002, the migration balance has fluctuated depending on the economic cycle. After a peak of 73,200 people in 2008 and a decline during the financial crisis, net immigration has recently increased again: in 2022 it was 52,900 people, in 2023 the number rose to 68,000, and in 2024 it fell to 53,700 people (p. 27, 28, 29). In 2024, 71% of EU/EFTA citizens immigrated to take up employment (p. 29).
*   **Immigration from third countries:** The migration balance of third-country nationals remained more stable compared to EU/EFTA citizens, with an average annual net immigration of 23,600 people between 2002 and 2024 (p. 29, 30). Here, immigration is less influenced by the labor market (only 8.5% to 11.3% between 2008 and 2024) and primarily by family reunification (41.6% to 51.6%) as well as education and training (18.1% to 21.7%) (p. 29).
*   **Asylum area:** Immigration is strongly dependent on international crises here (p. 30). In 2024, 27,740 asylum applications were filed (a decrease of 8.2% compared to 2023), with a protection rate of 54% (p. 30). Additionally, since 2022, over 100,000 people from Ukraine have received protection status S, of which 68,000 people still had an active status at the end of 2024 (p. 30).
*   **Overall population growth:** The permanent resident population was 8.96 million people at the end of December 2023 (p. 32). Between 2001 and 2023, the population grew by an average of around 77,600 people per year, with 80% of this growth due to the positive migration balance (p. 31). According to a reference scenario from the Federal Statistical Office from 2025, the population is expected to increase to 9.5 million by 2030 and exceed the ten million mark in 2041 (p. 32).

The adoption of the initiative would jeopardize the Bilateral II agreements, in particular the Schengen Association Agreement (SAA) and the Dublin Association Agreement (DAA) (p. 66).

Although these agreements are not formally linked to the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons (FZA) by a guillotine clause, the EU has repeatedly established a political connection between the FZA and the Schengen and Dublin association agreements (p. 66).

According to the dispatch, the loss of these agreements would have the following consequences:

*   **Economic impact:** The gross domestic product could be 1.6-3.7 percent lower by 2030, and per capita income could decrease by 700-1600 francs, depending on the scenario (p. 67). Furthermore, the tourism sector and border regions would be particularly affected by the loss of travel facilitations and the introduction of systematic border controls (p. 67).
*   **Asylum system:** Switzerland would no longer be able to carry out Dublin transfers, which would likely lead to an increase in repeat applications (p. 67). This would make the asylum system more expensive; the estimated annual additional costs would be around 220 million francs, with the costs of processing repeat applications ranging from 109 million to 1.1 billion francs (p. 67).
*   **Internal security:** Additional annual costs of up to 500 million francs would arise to compensate for the loss of the DAA and SAA (p. 67). The Federal Council points out that full compensation would be impossible, as certain data can only be obtained through the Schengen area (p. 67). Withdrawal from the European security area would significantly impede the guarantee of internal security (p. 4).

The popular initiative "Keine 10-Millionen-Schweiz! (Nachhaltigkeitsinitiative)" demands that the permanent resident population of Switzerland does not exceed the ten-million threshold before the year 2050 (p. 2, p. 7).

If the permanent resident population of Switzerland does not again comply with the ten million limit after two years have elapsed since it was first exceeded and no exception or safeguard clauses could be negotiated or invoked by then, with which compliance with the limit value is achieved, the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons (AFMP) with the EU is to be terminated on the next possible date (p. 2, 7, 37, 62).

The Federal Council justifies the endangerment of prosperity with the following points:

*   **Importance of the FZA:** The Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons (FZA) is of central importance for the Swiss economy and the securing of jobs (p. 64). It enables companies to have flexible and unbureaucratic access to a large pool of workers in the EU, which has contributed to covering the need for workers and to favourable economic development (p. 3).
*   **Demographic change:** Due to the advancing demographic ageing, Switzerland will also be dependent on foreign workers in the future to secure the innovative power, the competitiveness of the economy and the maintenance of the healthcare system (p. 3). A cancellation of the FZA would significantly reduce the growth potential of the economy (p. 66).
*   **Guillotine clause:** A termination of the FZA would automatically lead to the cancellation of further internal market agreements (Bilateral I) due to the guillotine clause, including agreements on public procurement, trade in agricultural products and land and air transport (p. 66). This would, according to the Federal Council, result in significantly weaker economic growth, a loss of legal certainty and a reduction in the attractiveness of the location (p. 66).

In summary, the Federal Council is of the opinion that the termination of the FZA and the associated cancellation of further bilateral agreements would have significant financial, economic and social consequences (p. 4).

If the permanent resident population of Switzerland exceeds the ten million limit and this is still not complied with after two years (and no exception or protective clauses apply), the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons (AFMP) with the EU must be terminated on the next possible date (p. 2, p. 8, p. 38, p. 63).

The effects on the economy would be severe according to the Federal Council:

*   **Loss of Bilaterals I:** Due to the so-called guillotine clause, a termination of the AFMP would automatically lead to the loss of other internal market agreements, including agreements on public procurement, trade in agricultural products, the elimination of technical trade barriers, and land and air transport (p. 3, p. 66). This would result in significantly weaker economic growth, a loss of legal certainty, and reduced location attractiveness (p. 66).
*   **Endangerment of Bilaterals II:** The Schengen and Dublin association agreements would also be endangered (p. 3, p. 66). A loss of these agreements could lead to a decline in gross domestic product (GDP) of 1.6 to 3.7 percent by 2030 and a decrease in per capita income of 700 to 1600 francs (p. 67). Additionally, the tourism sector and border regions would be negatively affected (p. 67).
*   **Labour market:** Since the Swiss economy relies on foreign workers, a loss of the AFMP would significantly reduce the growth potential of the economy and exacerbate the challenges of demographic change (p. 65).
*   **Additional financial costs:**
    *   In the **asylum sector**, annual additional costs of around 220 million francs would have to be expected, as no Dublin returns would be possible and more second applications would be expected (p. 4, p. 67).
    *   In the area of **internal security**, additional annual costs of up to 500 million francs could arise, whereby a complete compensation for the loss of data from the Schengen area would not be technically possible (p. 67).
*   **Trade and transport:** There would be significant delays in passenger and goods traffic, as well as increased complexity and uncertainty for companies that rely on efficient supply chains (p. 71).

The dispatch makes the following statements regarding the effects of limiting the population to ten million on housing shortages:

*   **Connection between immigration and housing market:** Immigration is referred to as the main driver for the increasing demand for living space (p. 35). Population growth leads to a strongly increasing demand encountering a barely growing supply, resulting in decreasing vacancy rates and rising prices for rental apartments and residential property (p. 35).

*   **Plans to solve the problem:** The Federal Council has defined various measures to address the scarce housing supply:
    *   **Financial promotion:** The Federal Council wants to increase the fund for promoting non-profit housing construction ("Fonds de roulement") by a total of 150 million francs over five years from 2030 (p. 74).
    *   **Tightening of the "Lex Koller" (BewG):** The conditions under which foreign nationals can acquire land or rights to it are to be tightened. This particularly concerns the acquisition of commercial property, the acquisition of main residences by non-EU/EFTA citizens, as well as potentially the acquisition of holiday apartments and residential units in apartment hotels (p. 77).
    *   **Action plan:** There is an "action plan against housing shortages" agreed upon in February 2024 with over 30 measures, in which cantons, cities, municipalities, and the construction and real estate industry are involved (p. 78).

The dispatch describes the difference with regard to flexibility as follows:

*   **Current practice:** The Federal Council considers neutrality as an instrument of security, foreign and economic policy that it has always flexibly further developed in the interest of Switzerland and taking into account the international environment and developments under international law (p. 5, p. 20). This flexibility has proven itself in 175 years of constitutional practice (p. 2).
*   **Proposal of the initiative:** The initiative wants to anchor a specific understanding and a specific design of neutrality directly in the Federal Constitution (p. 2, p. 13). According to the Federal Council, this would lead to a "rigid understanding of neutrality" (p. 2, p. 27) and mean a departure from the proven flexibility (p. 2).

**Consequences of the difference:**
The Federal Council argues that by anchoring it in the Constitution, the scope for flexible use of neutrality to safeguard national interests would be largely lost (p. 22). Any substantial adaptation to new circumstances or foreign policy challenges would in future only be possible through a constitutional revision, which would lead to a significant delay in responses (p. 2, p. 23).

According to the dispatch, neutrality plays the following role for Switzerland's good offices:

*   **Current status and practice:** Good offices are considered an active peace contribution that gives Swiss neutrality a "certain universal function" (p. 10). They are an essential part of neutrality policy (p. 21).
*   **Importance of neutrality:** Although neutrality is not an indispensable prerequisite for these activities – as factors such as political weight, discretion, and multilateral competencies are also important – it contributes to the credibility of the commitment and is one of several location advantages of Switzerland (p. 21).

In the **popular initiative**, this is dealt with as follows:

*   **Constitutional anchoring:** The popular initiative wants to explicitly stipulate in a new Article 54a, paragraph 4 E-BV that Switzerland should use its permanent neutrality for the prevention and resolution of conflicts and make itself available as a mediator (p. 14).
*   **Objective:** This is intended to ensure that Switzerland is respected worldwide as a steadfast and reliable neutral country and makes itself available as a mediator (p. 13).

The Federal Council notes that the demand to take on the role of mediator corresponds to current practice, and the explicit stipulation of this objective in itself would have no implications for neutrality policy (p. 21). However, it states that the popular initiative would strongly restrict or make impossible peace-promoting cooperation due to its other restrictions (particularly with regard to security policy cooperation), which would mean a departure from the previous active peace policy (p. 25).

The dispatch assesses the effects of the neutrality initiative on sanctions policy as a clear change in course with negative consequences (p. 2). The comparison between current practice and the initiative is as follows:

**Current Practice**
*   **Flexibility:** The Federal Council decides on a case-by-case basis whether to adopt international sanctions in whole, in part, or not at all, weighing foreign policy, foreign economic policy, and legal criteria (p. 18, 25).
*   **Scope:** Switzerland adopts sanctions decided by the UN, OSCE, or important trading partners (especially the EU) that serve to uphold international law (p. 18). Since joining the UN in 2002, the adoption of UN sanctions has been mandatory (p. 11, 21).
*   **Example:** Switzerland has largely adopted EU sanctions against Russia since February 2022 (p. 25).

**Effects of the Initiative**
*   **Restriction:** The initiative prohibits non-military coercive measures (sanctions) against warring states, with the exception of obligations towards the UN (p. 14, 18).
*   **Consequences for Cooperation:** The adoption of sanctions by the EU, OSCE, or other important trading partners against warring states would be excluded (p. 25). Specifically, sanctions like those taken against Russia since February 2022 would no longer be possible (p. 25).
*   **Scope for Action and Reputation:** Switzerland's scope for action would be strongly restricted (p. 2, 25). This could lead to reputational damage as well as foreign policy, security policy, and economic consequences, particularly if Switzerland were the only Western European country not to support EU sanctions against warring states (p. 3, 25).
*   **Legal Uncertainties and Paradoxes:**
    *   It is unclear whether existing embargo measures (e.g., against Russia) would have to be lifted or only no new ones adopted (p. 25).
    *   A paradox would arise with states that were initially not at war (and against which sanctions were imposed), but later became parties to the conflict (e.g., Iran); in such cases, sanctions might have to be lifted when the war begins (p. 25).
*   **Problem of Preventing Circumvention:** Although the initiative allows measures to prevent circumvention of other states' sanctions (p. 14, 18), the dispatch describes the effective monitoring and prevention of complex modern sanction regimes (such as those of the EU against Russia) without adopting the sanctions itself as a "Herculean task" (p. 27). This could meet with incomprehension from trading partners and have negative political and economic effects (p. 27).

The Federal Council recommends the rejection of the initiative, as it would overall lead to a clear change of course in Swiss neutrality, which would have negative effects on Switzerland's security, economic and foreign policy (p. 2).

In detail, the Federal Council cites the following reasons:

*   **Loss of flexibility:** The initiative demands a departure from the flexibility that has been proven for 175 years in the application of neutrality (p. 2). A rigid understanding of neutrality would make it more difficult to adapt neutrality to new circumstances and foreign policy challenges (p. 2, p. 20, p. 28).
*   **Weakening of defence capability:** Security and defence policy cooperation with military and defence alliances would be severely restricted (p. 2, p. 23). This would weaken Switzerland's defence capability, as exchange, joint training and procurement with partners (especially in NATO and the EU) are essential (p. 24, p. 28).
*   **Negative consequences for the arms industry:** The reliability of Switzerland as a supplier of armaments and components would be called into question, which would weaken the Swiss arms industry location (p. 2, p. 25, p. 28).
*   **Restriction of sanctions policy:** By prohibiting the adoption of certain non-military coercive measures (sanctions) outside the UN, Switzerland's scope for action would be severely restricted (p. 2, p. 25). This could result in reputational damage as well as foreign, security and economic policy consequences (p. 3, p. 25, p. 28).
*   **Impairment of peace policy:** Peace-promoting cooperation would be severely restricted or made impossible, which would mean a departure from the previously active peace policy practice (p. 26).

The current legal anchoring of neutrality is structured as follows according to the dispatch:

*   **Swiss law:** In the Federal Constitution (BV), neutrality is mentioned in the competence order of the federal authorities; the Federal Council and the Federal Assembly shall take "measures to safeguard [...] the neutrality of Switzerland" (Art. 173 para. 1 lit. a and 185 para. 1 BV) (p. 6). However, the BV does not define substantively what the neutrality of Switzerland is (p. 6). Various federal laws also refer to neutrality without defining it substantively (p. 6).
*   **International law:** The permanent neutrality of Switzerland was recognized under international law in 1815 at the Paris Peace Conference and has since been part of customary international law; this was last confirmed in 2002 when joining the UN (p. 6). As a permanently neutral state, Switzerland is neutral in all military conflicts between states (p. 6). The rights and obligations of a neutral state (law of neutrality) were codified in 1907 in two Hague Conventions, which Switzerland acceded to in 1910 (p. 6).
*   **Relationship between international and national law:** Due to the monistic system, international law applies directly in Switzerland (p. 8). The Federal Court assumes the fundamental primacy of international law (p. 8).
The Federal Chancellery established by decision of 28 May 2024 that the initiative was successful with 129,806 valid signatures (p. 4).

On the occasion of Switzerland's accession to the UN in 2002, Switzerland explicitly stated in its application for accession that it would maintain its neutrality, thus securing its parallel obligations under neutrality law and the UN Charter (p. 8). Furthermore, since this accession, Switzerland has been obliged to adopt UN sanctions (p. 11).

According to the initiative text, cooperation with military or defence alliances is only reserved or permitted as an exception in the following two cases:
*   in the event of a direct military attack on Switzerland (p. 2, 4, 14),
*   in the event of actions preparing such an attack (p. 2, 4, 14).

According to the Federal Council, the adoption of the initiative would have the following effects on Switzerland's security policy cooperation:

*   **Severe restriction of cooperation:** The initiative would mean a change in security policy course, with a significant restriction on security and defence policy cooperation (p. 2, 23). For example, Switzerland could hardly participate in NATO cooperation projects, such as training specialist personnel in the event of cyber attacks (p. 23).
*   **Weakening of defence capabilities:** Since exchange, exercises, joint training, and procurement with partners (mainly NATO and EU) are essential, restricting this cooperation would weaken Switzerland's defence capabilities (p. 2, 24).
*   **Loss of information:** Switzerland would be excluded from cooperation with military alliances, including the exchange of information and situation reports. This could lead to missing information about preparations for an attack on Switzerland (p. 24).
*   **Negative consequences for the arms industry:** International arms cooperation would be more severely restricted, which would call into question the reliability of Switzerland as a supplier of armaments and components, and weaken the Swiss arms industry. This would have negative consequences for the army's supply security (p. 2, 25).
*   **Impairment of peace policy:** Peace-promoting cooperation would also be severely restricted or even made impossible, which would mean a departure from the previous active peace policy practice (p. 26).
*   **Loss of credibility:** The restrictions would run counter to Switzerland's security policy interests and independence, and damage its credibility as an autonomous security policy actor (p. 24).

In summary, the Federal Council considers a security policy solo effort under waiver of international cooperation not to be a viable path (p. 24).

The Federal Council recommends rejecting the initiative not because of the anchoring of perpetual and armed neutrality – as this is already recognized under international law today and the Federal Council has always committed to it (p. 20, 21) – but because the initiative would overall lead to a rigid design of neutrality.

The reasons for rejection are:

*   **Loss of flexibility:** The initiative would end the proven practice of flexibly adapting neutrality as an instrument of security, foreign, and economic policy to the international environment (p. 2, 20, 22).
*   **Weakening of defense capability:** The strong restrictions on security policy cooperation with military and defense alliances would weaken Switzerland's defense capability (p. 2, 23, 24). The Federal Council sees a conflict of objectives here: a credible enforcement of armed neutrality requires military competencies that would be endangered by the required restrictions on cooperation (p. 27).
*   **Restriction of sanctions policy:** The ban on taking non-military coercive measures against warring states (except for UN sanctions) would strongly restrict the scope for action. This could lead to reputational damage as well as foreign, security, and economic policy consequences (p. 2, 3, 25).
*   **Negative consequences for the arms industry:** The reliability of Switzerland as a supplier of armaments and components would be called into question, which could weaken the Swiss arms industry (p. 2, 24, 25).
*   **Impairment of peace policy:** Peace-promoting cooperation (e.g., within the framework of NATO-led missions such as in Kosovo) would be strongly restricted or made impossible (p. 26).

The initiative does not hinder Switzerland from acting as a mediator; on the contrary, it wants to explicitly enshrine this.

According to the wording of the initiative (Art. 54a para. 4 E-BV), Switzerland shall use its permanent neutrality for the prevention and resolution of conflicts and make itself available as a mediator (p. 4).

The initiative committee holds the view that Switzerland, through the anchoring of an "unrestricted" understanding of neutrality in the Constitution, would be respected by all countries as steadfast and reliable neutral and thus be available as a mediator (p. 13). Furthermore, the initiators argue that this understanding represents an added value for Swiss peace policy, including the "good offices" (p. 14).

The Federal Council notes that the demand to take on the role of mediator and use neutrality for peacekeeping already corresponds to federal council practice today (p. 22).

If the initiative is accepted, Switzerland may fundamentally not impose non-military coercive measures (sanctions) against warring states (p. 4, 14).

However, there are two exceptions reserved in the initiative text (p. 4, 14):
*   **Obligations towards the UN:** Switzerland should continue to fulfil its obligations as a member state of the United Nations Organisation (UN) (p. 4, 14, 18).
*   **Prevention of circumventions:** Measures to prevent the circumvention of non-military coercive measures by other states remain possible (p. 4, 14).

The Federal Council explains that with the acceptance of the initiative, the adoption of sanctions by the EU, the OSCE or further important trading partners against warring states would be excluded (p. 25).

The initiative and the Federal Council assess the impact on the role of Switzerland as a mediator differently:

*   **Position of the initiative committee:** The committee wants to enshrine in the Federal Constitution that Switzerland uses its permanent neutrality for the prevention and resolution of conflicts and is available as a mediator (p. 2, 4). This should represent an added value for peace policy (including "good services") as well as the multilateral orientation of foreign policy (p. 14).
*   **Position of the Federal Council:**
    *   The Federal Council states that the perception of the mediator role and the use of neutrality for peacekeeping already correspond to today's practice (p. 22). Neutrality is not an indispensable prerequisite for these activities, but it contributes to the credibility of the commitment (p. 22).
    *   At the same time, the Federal Council warns that the initiative would strongly restrict or make impossible peace-promoting cooperation (e.g., participation in the NATO-led Kosovo troops), which would mean a departure from the previous active peace policy practice (p. 26).
    *   Furthermore, the Federal Council doubts that the rigid understanding of neutrality demanded by the initiators would actually lead to international respect as a mediator. For neutrality to be respected, it must be perceived as comprehensible and useful, which requires active contributions to international order (p. 27).

The objectives of the tax fairness initiative and the indirect counter-proposal (Federal Act on Individual Taxation) are:

*   the civil status-independent taxation and thus also the abolition of the so-called marriage penalty,
*   the increase in employment incentives for second earners and
*   the improvement of equal opportunities for women and men (p. 3).

The taxation of married couples differs between the current law and the proposed individual taxation as follows:

**Current Law**
*   **System:** The community taxation applies, where the family is considered an economic unit (p. 10).
*   **Income treatment:** The incomes of legally and actually undivided spouses are combined regardless of the marital property regime (factor addition) (p. 10).
*   **Tariffs:** A multiple tariff system exists with a basic tariff for singles, a married couples' tariff, and a parents' tariff (p. 10).
*   **Reliefs:** To mitigate the progressive effect of factor addition, a married couples' deduction and a dual-income earner deduction are granted (p. 10).
*   **Procedure and liability:** Spouses are jointly assessed; there is joint and several liability for the tax debt (p. 10, 39).

**Proposed Individual Taxation**
*   **System:** Married couples are taxed individually like unmarried couples (p. 3, 24).
*   **Income treatment:** Income and assets are assigned to individual spouses according to civil law relationships or other statutory entitlements (p. 24, 25).
*   **Tariffs:** The multiple tariff is replaced by a uniform tariff that applies to all natural persons regardless of their marital status (p. 72).
*   **Reliefs:**
    *   The married couples' deduction and the dual-income earner deduction are abolished (p. 68, 71).
    *   Child-related deductions are generally divided equally between parents (p. 3, 24, 32).
    *   The child deduction for direct federal tax is increased from 6,700 to 12,000 francs (p. 3, 24, 31).
*   **Procedure and liability:** Married couples fill out two separate tax returns (p. 3, 24, 37). Joint and several liability is abolished; each person is liable only for their own tax (p. 39).

The individual taxation increases the employment incentives for second earners, as when taking up gainful employment or increasing the second income, a significantly lower tax burden is incurred compared to today's joint taxation (p. 3).

This is due to the following mechanisms according to the Federal Council:
* **Marginal tax rate:** In a progressive tax system, individual taxation leads to a significantly lower marginal tax rate for the second income (p. 96). In contrast, with today's joint taxation, the second income is taxed based on the progression stage of the first income, which increases the burden (p. 96).
* **Independence:** In the reform scenario, the marginal tax rate for the second income is independent of the amount of the first income (p. 100).

**Positions of the actors:**
* **Federal Council:** It sees in these employment effects a better exploitation of the domestic labour and skilled worker potential, which would trigger a macroeconomic impulse (p. 3, 18, 20).
* **Initiative committee:** They argue that the current system keeps well-educated women away from the labour market in particular. Individual taxation sets the right incentives to remedy the shortage of skilled workers and increase equal opportunities (p. 15).
* **Supporters (certain parties, cantons, and organisations):** They are of the opinion that individual taxation creates high employment incentives for second earners and thus promotes equal opportunities for women and men (p. 21).
* **Opponents (certain parties, cantons, and organisations):** They doubt the employment effects and argue that the decision to take up gainful employment depends primarily on non-tax factors such as job offers or childcare options (p. 21).

The Federal Council rejects the popular initiative and instead proposes an indirect counter-proposal, as this way the goal of civil status-independent taxation can be achieved more quickly (p. 3).

The Federal Council gives the following reasons in particular (p. 17):

*   **Implementation speed:** The introduction of individual taxation is also possible without a provision at constitutional level, whereby the route via legislation leads to the goal more quickly.
*   **Restriction of the legislature:** Anchoring the tax method (whether joint or individual) in the constitution would restrict the legislature.
*   **Existing preliminary work:** A corresponding bill was already being drafted, as the parliament had commissioned the Federal Council in the context of the 2019-2023 legislative planning to submit a proposal for the introduction of individual taxation.
*   **Need for further measures:** Although anchoring in the constitution would mean a binding decision on direction, measures to implement the new constitutional provision would still be required, whereby the elimination of the marriage penalty has been pending for around 40 years.

The estimated reduced revenues from direct federal tax amount to around 1 billion francs per year with reference to the tax year 2024 (p. 3, p. 25). Of this, the Confederation bears around 800 million francs and the cantons around 200 million francs (p. 3, p. 25).
Nationally, there are approximately 1.7 million additional tax returns to be expected (p. 3, p. 44).

The introduction of individual taxation has the following effects on the tariff codes of withholding tax:

*   **Adjustment and deletion:** The withholding tax tariffs and thus the tariff codes must be adjusted. Previous tariff codes are deleted, in particular the code for dual-income earners (p. 41, 45).
*   **Reasons for adjustment:** The necessity arises from the increase in child deductions, tariff adjustments, and the abolition of certain deductions, namely the married couple's deduction and the dual-income earner's deduction (p. 41).
*   **New tariff codes:** For each new ordinary withholding tax tariff, new tariff codes must be created for German and Italian cross-border commuters (p. 45).

In married couples without children with an uneven distribution of income of 90/10, additional burdens result in most of the constellations presented (p. 82). These additional burdens occur from a total income of the married couple of around 30,000 francs (p. 82).

Concrete examples for the tax burden in this constellation (90/10, without children) in comparison between status quo and reform are listed in Table 1 (p. 85):
*   With a total income of 40,000 francs, the burden increases from 0 to 99 francs.
*   With 70,000 francs, it increases from 312 to 508 francs.
*   With 100,000 francs, it increases from 1,198 to 1,692 francs.
*   With 150,000 francs, it increases from 4,116 to 5,562 francs.
*   With 250,000 francs, it increases from 16,113 to 16,167 francs.

The Federal Council pursues the following objectives and reasons with the introduction of individual taxation and the associated abolition of the marriage penalty:

*   **Incentives to work and national economy:** Individual taxation is intended to increase incentives to work, particularly for second earners (mostly women) (p. 3). This would lead to better utilization of the domestic labor and skilled workforce potential and trigger a national economic impulse (p. 4).
*   **Equality and social security:** The measure is intended to strengthen the financial independence of both spouses as well as their provision for old age and in the event of divorce, which contributes to equality between women and men (p. 3, 4). This is in line with the more recent case law of the Federal Court on the principle of self-sufficiency after a divorce (p. 4).
*   **Independence from marital status:** The goal is taxation independent of marital status, where it is irrelevant whether a person is married, divorced, widowed, or single (p. 3, 15).

Regarding the financial impact and distribution of relief, the Federal Council states:
*   **Reduced revenue:** The Federal Council accepts the estimated reduced revenue of around 1 billion francs per year (related to the 2024 tax year) (p. 3).
*   **Distribution of relief:** The relief is distributed across all income classes (p. 4). Although married persons with a rather equal distribution of income benefit in particular (p. 3), the Federal Council wants to prevent the relief effect from concentrating on the highest incomes through targeted tariff adjustments, in order to achieve a more even distribution across all income classes (p. 34, 35). Furthermore, most unmarried persons without children are relieved through the tariff adjustment (p. 3).

The Federal Council justifies the promotion of equal rights for women and men through individual taxation as follows:

*   **Incentives to work and financial independence:** Individual taxation increases the incentives to work for secondary earners (namely women), as the tax burden when taking up gainful employment or increasing the second income is significantly lower than with today's joint taxation (p. 3, 4, 103). This strengthens the financial independence of both spouses as well as their provision for old age and in the event of a divorce (p. 4, 103).
*   **Economic impulse:** The better incentives will make better use of the domestic labor and skilled workforce potential, triggering an economic impulse (p. 4).
*   **Jurisprudence:** This development is in line with the more recent jurisprudence of the Federal Court on post-marital maintenance, which emphasizes the principle of self-sufficiency after a divorce (p. 4, 103).

Regarding the tax burden and distribution, the Federal Council states:

*   **General burden:** The proportion of taxpayers who experience a reduction in their tax burden is significantly greater than the proportion of those with an increased burden (p. 3). The lowest incomes as well as families with medium incomes will continue to pay no direct federal tax (p. 3).
*   **Increased burdens:** The Federal Council acknowledges that the reform can lead to increased burdens, particularly for married couples with only one income or a low second income, especially when children are present and the incomes are in the middle and higher classes (p. 3, 4).
*   **Balancing performance capacity:** The Federal Council recognizes a field of tension with the principle of taxation according to economic performance capacity, as for example in the case of single-earner married couples, the child deduction is divided equally, even though one person may be solely responsible for maintenance (p. 106). However, it justifies this with the aim of making the tax assessment as uncomplicated as possible, which requires schematic solutions (p. 106).

The individual taxation has the following effects on women who work alongside their partner:

*   **Increase of employment incentives:** The introduction of individual taxation increases the employment incentives for secondary earners, from which women benefit primarily, as they achieve the second income in most cases (p. 3, 103).
*   **Facilitation of overtime:** It becomes easier for them to work more or take up gainful employment, as in this constellation a significantly lower tax burden would be incurred compared to today's joint taxation (p. 3, 103). The tax system would thus hinder the uptake or expansion of a second income less (p. 103).
*   **Financial and social consequences:** Through individual taxation, the financial independence of both spouses is strengthened. Furthermore, women's provision for old age and insurance in the event of divorce improve (p. 4, 103).

These assessments are represented by the Federal Council as well as by proponents of individual taxation (certain parties, cantons, and organisations) (p. 3, 21, 103).

With regard to married couples living separately, the following points can be gathered from the dispatch:

*   **Applicable law:** According to current law, married couples living separately are already assessed separately. In this case, the mutual right to inspect tax files is waived (p. 38).
*   **Indirect counter-proposal (planned individual taxation):**
    *   **General principle:** Taxation is carried out in a civil status-neutral manner, i.e., each person is taxed individually, regardless of their civil status (p. 3, p. 25).
    *   **Child deductions:** For parents living separately, it remains an exception that maintenance contributions for minor children can be deducted (p. 33).
*   **Complexity of tax returns:** The dispatch does not contain an explicit statement on whether the tax return will become simpler or more complex specifically for married couples living separately. However, it generally states that the introduction of individual taxation for married couples who were previously jointly taxed will result in greater effort, as both spouses must now submit their own tax return (p. 19, p. 44).

The positions of the initiative committee and the Federal Council on the compatibility of an import ban with international trade obligations are opposed to each other:

*   **Position of the initiative committee:** The committee represents the view that an import ban is compatible with Switzerland's international trade obligations (p. 7). As justification, it states that all agreements provide for exceptions for measures necessary to protect public morals and the life or health of animals (p. 7). Furthermore, it refers to existing import bans on dog, cat, and seal fur, as well as to the recognition by the highest court of the World Trade Organization (WTO) that animal protection is part of public morality (p. 7).

*   **Position of the Federal Council:** The Federal Council assesses an import ban as not compatible with Switzerland's international obligations and sees a risk of trade disputes (p. 2, 16). Its assessment is based on the following points:
    *   **WTO law:** An import ban would be the most drastic measure in international trade. Since it would be introduced without prior milder measures (such as a declaration requirement), it would likely not withstand a WTO-law proportionality test and would violate GATT and the TBT Agreement (p. 11, 14).
    *   **EU agreements:** The ban would violate the free trade agreement with the EU, as it would fail to meet the proportionality requirement (p. 14). Furthermore, it would be in contradiction to the bilateral agricultural agreement, which grants Switzerland a tariff concession for an annual quantity of 20 tons of fatty livers from the EU (p. 15).

The Federal Council assesses the impact of adopting the Stopfleber initiative on international trade as follows:

*   **General assessment:** An import ban constitutes a serious interference with free trade, which is fundamentally incompatible with Switzerland's international obligations and entails the risk of international trade disputes and sanctions (p. 2, p. 10, p. 16).
*   **WTO obligations:** The Federal Council sees violations of the GATT (in particular the prohibition of quantitative trade restrictions according to Art. XI:1 and the prohibition of discrimination according to Art. I:1) as well as against the TBT Agreement (p. 12, p. 13, p. 14). Since an import ban is the most drastic measure, it would likely not withstand a WTO legal proportionality test without prior milder measures (e.g., a declaration requirement) (p. 11, p. 13, p. 14).
*   **Relationship with the EU:**
    *   **Free trade agreement:** The ban would violate the prohibition of new quantitative import restrictions (Art. 13) (p. 14). Furthermore, it could be considered as unjustified discrimination against France, since foie gras is declared a cultural heritage there (p. 14).
    *   **Agricultural agreement:** An import ban would contradict the intention to liberalize trade in agricultural products and would run counter to the specific customs concession granted by Switzerland to the EU for an annual quantity of 20 tons of foie gras (p. 15).
*   **Future impact:** The Federal Council warns that new trade barriers could make ongoing negotiations with the EU more difficult, particularly the planned expansion of the agricultural agreement to the entire food chain (p. 10, p. 11, p. 15, p. 16).

The Federal Council rejects the popular initiative for the following reasons:

*   **International obligations and trade risks:** An import ban would not be compatible with Switzerland's international obligations and would involve the risk of international trade disputes as well as sanctions (p. 2, 11). Specifically, it would violate WTO legal requirements (GATT and TBT Agreement), as quantitative trade restrictions and discriminations are prohibited (p. 12, 13, 14). Furthermore, it would violate the free trade agreement and the agricultural agreement with the EU, in particular a specific customs concession for foie gras (p. 14, 15).
*   **Proportionality and milder measures:** Import bans are serious interventions in free trade and should only be taken according to the principle of proportionality when milder measures have not achieved the goal (p. 2, 16). The Federal Council has already initiated a declaration obligation for foie gras, which is expected to come into force in summer 2025 (p. 2, 12, 16).
*   **Legal hierarchical justice:** An amendment to the Federal Constitution is not required, as the Animal Protection Act already provides the basis for such a ban (p. 9, 16). A ban at the constitutional level would not be hierarchically justifiable for such a particular concern (p. 12).
*   **Impact on EU relations:** Approval would affect trade relations and the free movement of goods with the EU (p. 9). Furthermore, new trade barriers could make ongoing negotiations on the extension of the agricultural agreement to the entire food chain more difficult (p. 11, 15, 16).
*   **Internal tensions:** Since foie gras is particularly popular in Romandy and Ticino, while being consumed significantly less in German-speaking Switzerland, emotional debates and tensions between language communities could arise (p. 12, 16).
*   **Enforcement and effectiveness:** Controlling imports, especially by private individuals, would be difficult, as only random samples could be checked (p. 11, 16). Moreover, the direct impact on animal welfare would be small, as Switzerland's demand accounts for only about 1 percent of the world market (p. 11).

In the event of the adoption of the initiative, this would have the following effects on consumers according to the Federal Council:

*   **Product selection and consumption:** Since foie gras and foie gras products would neither be allowed to be purchased domestically nor imported for private consumption and equivalent alternatives are lacking, the consumption of foie gras in Switzerland would be made impossible (p. 10).
*   **Regional impact:** These effects would particularly affect consumers in Romandy and Ticino, as significantly less foie gras is consumed in German-speaking Switzerland (p. 10).
*   **Social tensions:** The Federal Council points out that the ban could lead to emotional debates and tensions due to different consumption habits between language communities (p. 12, p. 16).

The Federal Council cites as reasons for the rejection of the import ban the incompatibility with the following international legal provisions and obligations:

*   **WTO legal obligations:**
    *   The **General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)** of 30 October 1947 (p. 13).
    *   The **Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT Agreement)** of 12 April 1979 (p. 13).
*   **Agreements with the EU:**
    *   The **Free Trade Agreement** of 22 July 1972 between Switzerland and the European Economic Community (p. 14).
    *   The **Agriculture Agreement** of 21 June 1999 between Switzerland and the European Community on trade in agricultural products (p. 14).
The popular initiative "Yes to the import ban on foie gras (foie gras initiative)" was submitted on 28 December 2023 (p. 2, p. 3).
The popular initiative "Yes to the import ban on foie gras (foie gras initiative)" has been launched with 102,478 valid signatures (p. 3).

The Federal Council decided on 5 April 2023 to initiate the introduction of a declaration requirement for stuffed liver and stuffed liver products (p. 2). In this context, it commissioned the Federal Department of the Interior (EDI) to draw up a regulatory proposal for a declaration requirement for stuffed liver and other products (p. 4, p. 12).

As in Switzerland, the stopfmast is banned in the following European countries: Denmark, Germany, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Poland, Sweden, and the Czech Republic (p. 6). Furthermore, the initiative committee states that stopfmast is no longer permitted in more than 20 other countries, including for example Norway, Israel, and Argentina (p. 7).

The Federal Council considers the concerns of the initiative to be comprehensible from an animal welfare perspective and holds the view that force-feeding is not compatible with the objectives of the Animal Welfare Act, which is why it has already been banned in Switzerland (p. 2, 9). However, it rejects an import ban for the following reasons:

*   **International obligations and trade risks:** An import ban would not be compatible with Switzerland's international obligations and would entail the risk of international trade disputes (p. 2). It would likely violate WTO legal requirements (GATT and TBT Agreement) since an import ban is the most drastic measure in international trade and would probably not withstand a proportionality test without prior milder measures (p. 11, 12, 14).
*   **Relations with the EU:** The adoption would affect trade relations and the free movement of goods with the EU (p. 9). Specifically, a ban would contradict the Agricultural Agreement, which grants Switzerland tariff concessions for an annual quantity of 20 tonnes of foie gras from the EU (p. 15). Furthermore, current negotiations to expand the Agricultural Agreement could be made more difficult (p. 11, 15).
*   **Proportionality and milder measures:** The Federal Council holds the view that import bans should only be imposed when all milder measures have not achieved their goal (p. 2, 16). It has therefore already initiated the introduction of a declaration requirement for foie gras (p. 2, 4, 16).
*   **Legal hierarchical justice:** An amendment to the Federal Constitution is not required since the Animal Welfare Act already provides the basis for such a ban (p. 9). A ban at the constitutional level would not be hierarchically justifiable for such a specific topic (p. 12).
*   **Domestic political tensions:** Since foie gras is mainly consumed in the Romandy and Ticino, emotional debates and tensions could arise between language communities (p. 12, 16).
*   **Enforcement and effect:** Controlling imports, particularly by private individuals, would be difficult (p. 11, 16). Moreover, the Federal Council estimates the direct impact on animal welfare to be minor since Switzerland accounts for only about 1 percent of global demand (p. 10, 11).

The Federal Council does not claim that an import ban is compatible with the international obligations. On the contrary: it represents the position that such a ban would **not** be compatible with the international obligations of Switzerland (p. 2) and would violate GATT as well as the TBT Agreement (p. 14).

For exactly this reason, the Federal Council assumes that an import ban would entail the risk of international trade disputes (p. 2, p. 16).

The view that an import ban is compatible with the international trade obligations of Switzerland, on the other hand, is represented by the **initiative committee** (p. 7).

The Federal Council recommends the rejection of the initiative for the following reasons (p. 1, p. 2):

*   **International obligations and trade risks:** An import ban would not be compatible with Switzerland's international obligations and would pose the risk of international trade disputes (p. 2). Specifically, it would likely violate WTO legal requirements (GATT and TBT Agreement), as an import ban is the most drastic measure and would probably not withstand a proportionality test without prior milder measures (such as a declaration requirement) (p. 11, p. 13, p. 14).
*   **Relations with the EU:** The ban would affect agreements with the EU (free trade and agricultural agreements), particularly since Switzerland is committed to granting tariff concessions for a certain quantity of foie gras (p. 14, p. 15). Furthermore, current negotiations to expand the agricultural agreement could be made more difficult (p. 15).
*   **Proportionality and alternatives:** According to the Federal Council, import bans should only be imposed when milder measures have not achieved their goal (p. 2, p. 16). It has therefore already initiated the introduction of a declaration requirement (p. 2, p. 16).
*   **Legal step-by-step justice:** An amendment to the Federal Constitution is not necessary, as the Animal Protection Act already provides the basis for such a ban (p. 9, p. 12, p. 16).
*   **Domestic political tensions:** Since foie gras is particularly popular in Romandy and Ticino, emotional debates and tensions between language communities could arise (p. 12, p. 16).
*   **Enforcement and effect:** Controlling imports, especially by private individuals, would be difficult (p. 11, p. 16). Furthermore, the Federal Council estimates the direct impact on animal welfare to be minor, as Switzerland accounts for only about 1 percent of global demand (p. 10, p. 11).

An import ban on foie gras could, according to the Federal Council, lead to problems with the EU for the following reasons:

*   **Violation of agreements:** Such a ban would violate the free trade agreement, which prohibits new quantitative import restrictions (p. 14). Although there are exceptions (e.g., for public morality or animal protection), the Federal Council assumes that the ban would fail due to the required proportionality (p. 14).
*   **Contradiction to the agricultural agreement:** The bilateral agricultural agreement aims at liberalizing trade in agricultural products. An import ban would contradict this intention and also violate a specific customs concession of Switzerland towards the EU for an annual quantity of 20 tons of foie gras (p. 15).
*   **Discrimination of cultural traditions:** Since foie gras has been declared a cultural heritage in France, a ban could be considered as unjustified discrimination against France due to its cultural traditions (p. 14).
*   **Obstruction of future negotiations:** The Federal Council and the EU Commission are currently negotiating the extension of the agricultural agreement to the entire food chain. An import ban would create new trade barriers that could make these negotiations more difficult (p. 11, p. 15, p. 16).
*   **Risk of countermeasures:** It is conceivable that the EU will take targeted countermeasures, such as refusing to update important bilateral agreements (p. 11).

The Federal Council assesses the deadline of ten years mentioned in the transitional provision as "short and rigid" and is of the opinion that the approach of the initiators goes too far with this (p. 3, p. 18).

In comparison to the existing measures, the Federal Council mentions the following points:

*   **Consequences of the deadline:** In order to comply with the short deadline, rigorous regulatory and incentive measures would have to be taken, which would be associated with unjustifiable or enormous economic and social costs as well as far-reaching negative consequences (p. 2, p. 3, p. 14, p. 15).
*   **Advantage of existing measures:** In contrast to the initiative, the path already taken (existing constitutional provisions and measures) allows for a "pragmatic and flexible approach" (p. 14).
*   **Suitability:** The Federal Council considers the applicable provisions as well as the goals and measures already set to be better suited to finding sustainable solutions together with the affected parties (p. 18). According to the Federal Council, the implementation of the initiative would undermine the efforts for a careful development of solutions, as this process requires time and the involvement of the parties concerned (p. 3).

The Federal Council sees the following effects on the economy in the event of the adoption of the Environmental Responsibility Initiative compared to the existing measures:

*   **Costs and prosperity:** While the existing measures and instruments are not associated with drastic economic consequences (p. 9), the initiative would be associated with unacceptable and disproportionate costs for the economy and society (p. 2, p. 3). The Federal Council warns that the population's prosperity would drastically decrease as a result (p. 15, p. 17).
*   **Regulation and economic freedom:** Due to the short transition period of ten years, rigorous or drastic regulatory and incentive measures would have to be taken, according to the Federal Council, which would restrict economic freedom (p. 3, p. 16).
*   **Investments and production:** High investments for product developments as well as a high financial outlay for the rapid modernization of production factors (especially machines) would be expected (p. 3, p. 17). Primarily affected would be agriculture, the food industry, the textile industry, and the construction and real estate sector (p. 17).
*   **Competitiveness and SMEs:** Companies could suffer a competitive disadvantage on the foreign market due to higher production costs, which would particularly affect SMEs (p. 16). Furthermore, a high use of tax revenue would reduce the tax attractiveness of Switzerland (p. 17).
*   **Trade and imports:** The Federal Council expects that the import of environmentally harmful goods would have to be more strongly regulated, which would increase the costs for imports and potentially worsen the competitiveness of the economy (p. 17). Additionally, long-term foreign trade relations could suffer and Switzerland's negotiating position vis-à-vis trading partners could be weakened (p. 17).
*   **Market effects:** Price increases, a decreasing variety of offerings, and a smaller product selection can be expected (p. 3, p. 18).

In contrast, the Federal Council is of the opinion that the already existing constitutional provisions and initiated measures are better suited because they allow for a pragmatic and flexible approach (p. 14).

The positions of the Federal Council and the initiators differ as follows:

*   **The initiators** demand a constitutional anchoring (Art. 94a BV), according to which the Swiss overall economy must necessarily act within the framework of nature and its renewability (p. 2, 12). They demand that the environmental pollution caused by consumption in Switzerland does not exceed the planetary limits (measured by the population share) at the latest ten years after the adoption of the initiative (p. 2, 4, 12). In case of conflict, ecology should take precedence over economy (p. 12). They also demand a socially acceptable design, in which particularly wealthy people and corporations take on greater responsibility (p. 12).

*   **The Federal Council** represents the view that this approach goes too far (p. 3, 14). In particular, it describes the deadline of ten years as too short and rigid (p. 3, 18). It argues that compliance with this deadline would require rigorous measures that would lead to disproportionate costs for society and economy, drastic losses of prosperity, price increases, and a restricted range of services (p. 3, 15, 16). The Federal Council considers the existing constitutional provisions on sustainability to be balanced (p. 7, 19) and prefers a pragmatic, flexible approach as well as the continuation of ongoing legislative and strategic processes over the strict requirements of the initiative (p. 3, 14, 19).

The Federal Council recommends the rejection of the Environmental Responsibility Initiative for the following reasons:

*   **Disproportionate costs and economic consequences:** The initiative would be associated with unbearable or enormous macroeconomic and social costs (p. 2, 3, 14, 19). The prosperity of the population would drastically decrease (p. 15, 17).
*   **Short implementation period:** In particular, the ten-year deadline mentioned in the transitional provision is too short and too rigid for the Federal Council (p. 2, 3). This would necessitate rigorous regulatory and incentive measures as well as drastic instruments (p. 3, 15).
*   **Effects on the economy:**
    *   There would be a restriction of economic freedom (p. 17).
    *   Companies, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), could suffer a competitive disadvantage in foreign markets due to higher production costs for the Swiss market (p. 3, 17).
    *   High investments in product developments would have to be made and machines would have to be modernized more quickly than usual (p. 3, 17).
    *   There would be trade policy risks and potential conflicts with international obligations (e.g., GATT, free trade agreements with the EU) (p. 17, 18).
*   **Effects on society:**
    *   Price increases, a decrease in the variety of offerings, and a restriction of consumer choice can be expected (p. 3, 16).
    *   Structural changes in companies could lead to job losses and exacerbate social inequalities (p. 16).
*   **Burden on the state:** Significant additional expenditures and massive enforcement costs would arise for the Confederation, cantons, and municipalities (p. 15).
*   **Limited environmental benefits abroad:** The environmental benefits in the countries of production would be limited compared to the costs, as Swiss demand alone has only a modest influence (p. 14).
*   **Sufficiency of existing regulations:** The Federal Council is of the opinion that the existing constitutional provisions on sustainability are already balanced and do not require supplementation (p. 7, 19). Furthermore, the initiative would undermine the careful development of sustainable and socially acceptable solutions, which requires time and the involvement of affected stakeholders (p. 3).

The existing constitutional provisions on sustainability play a central role in the dispatch as a justification for the Federal Council's recommendation for rejection.

The Federal Council represents the following positions and cites the following points:

*   **Existing legal basis:** There is already a constitutional basis for considering global sustainability through Articles 2, 54, 73, 74, 104, and 104a of the Federal Constitution (BV) as well as the preamble (p. 7).
    *   **Art. 2 para. 2 and 4 BV:** Require the promotion of sustainable development and the lasting preservation of natural foundations of life as state objectives (p. 7).
    *   **Art. 73 BV:** Anchors the principle of sustainability by striving for a permanently balanced relationship between the renewability of nature and its use by humans (p. 7).
    *   **Art. 74 BV:** Serves as a general competence and task norm in environmental protection (p. 7).
    *   **Art. 104 para. 1 and Art. 104a BV:** Relate to sustainable agricultural production or resource-conserving handling of food (p. 7).
    *   **Art. 54 para. 2 and Art. 104a letter d BV:** Define the preservation of natural foundations of life as a goal of foreign policy or demand sustainable cross-border trade relations in agriculture and food economy (p. 7).
*   **Evaluation of the provisions:** The Federal Council considers the existing provisions to be "balanced" (p. 7, p. 19). They would give the legislature sufficient leeway to respond to developments (p. 7, p. 19).
*   **Demarcation from the initiative:**
    *   While the existing Art. 73 BV provides for a weighing of interests, the proposed Art. 94a BV would give ecology priority over economy in case of conflict and waive such a weighing (p. 12).
    *   The Federal Council argues that the current path via the existing provisions enables a "pragmatic and flexible approach" (p. 14) and is "better suited" to finding sustainable solutions together with affected stakeholders than the strict requirements of the initiative (p. 18).

For these reasons, the Federal Council sees no need for an amendment to the Constitution in the sense of the initiative and waives a direct counter-proposal (p. 19).

The Federal Council considers the effects on society in the event of the adoption of the initiative to be problematic, as the short transition period of ten years would require strong and rapid adjustments in the economy and consumption (p. 15). Specifically, it sees the following consequences:
